analysis.one_liner: Cuts methane waste and collects royalties on gas vented or flared on federal land.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced July 29, 2015 with 14 Democratic cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote and died when the 114th Congress ended January 3, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require oil and gas companies drilling on federal land to capture 99% of the gas they produce within five years, ban routine flaring by new wells, install meters on vented and flared gas, and post the data publicly. It would also require companies to pay royalties on gas they currently lose to venting, flaring, and leaks — gas that today escapes without payment. Currently, that royalty obligation generally applies only to gas that is removed or sold, so gas burned off or leaked from a well site produces no revenue for the federal treasury.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal and tribal taxpayers, who would collect royalties on gas that companies currently vent, flare, or lose to leaks for free. Communities near federal drilling sites would get less methane and volatile organic compounds in the air, plus public online access to data on how much gas each operator wastes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Federal taxpayers and communities near drilling sites

how_it_helps.text: Royalties would be assessed on all gas produced under federal mineral leases, including gas vented, flared, or lost to fugitive releases, with narrow exceptions for 48-hour health emergencies and gas reinjected underground.

Operators would have to capture 99% of gas produced on federal leases annually within five years of enactment, flare rather than vent when capture is not viable, and stop flaring at all new wells within two years.

Companies would have to install meters on vented and flared gas, run scheduled leak-detection surveys with infrared cameras, repair leaks found within two weeks, and keep the data publicly available online for free.
Unauthorized venting or flaring would carry civil penalties equivalent to three times the market value of the gas, plus possible production restrictions.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies operating on federal lands, which would bear the cost of capture equipment, meters, leak-detection programs, and new royalty payments on gas they currently waste.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers on federal land

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall on operators, and the bill applies only to new leases issued after enactment, so royalties on wasted gas would not be collected on existing leases.

Critics of capture mandates generally argue that requiring 99% capture and banning flaring can be uneconomic where pipelines do not exist, which could discourage some federal-lease drilling; the bill text itself contains no such argument, so this objection is based on standard industry positioning rather than the record.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core trade is straightforward: companies pay to capture, meter, and pay royalties on gas they now burn off or leak, and taxpayers collect revenue while nearby communities get cleaner air. Because royalties would apply only to future leases, the fiscal and environmental gains would be real but gradual. The bill does not include cost-sharing or phase-in flexibility beyond its own timelines, which is the strongest honest objection to its design.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Alan Lowenthal introduced the bill on July 29, 2015 with 12 original cosponsors; 14 Democrats cosponsored in total, with no Republicans.
It was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the day it was introduced, and to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources on August 31, 2015.
No further action was taken before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, so the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies operating on federal land are better off, because they avoided new capture, metering, and leak-repair requirements and continued to owe no royalties on gas they vent, flare, or lose to leaks. Federal taxpayers and people living near federal drilling sites did not get the royalties or the reductions in wasted gas the bill promised.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 14 cosponsors were Democrats, and the bill sat in a committee controlled by Republicans without action; no Republican supported it and no Republican action beyond non-scheduling appears in the record.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers on federal lands
industries.note: The bill would require these companies to capture 99% of produced gas, install meters and leak-detection programs, pay royalties on vented, flared, and leaked gas, and face penalties of three times market value for unauthorized flaring or venting. The industry's interest in blocking the bill ran directly against the royalty revenue and air-quality gains for the public. Note: because the bill only applies to leases issued after enactment, its revenue effect would be limited to future leases.
